docs.title: prompts.py
docs.text: Source: utils/prompts.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
Building directly upon the telemetry and messaging infrastructure provided by utils/output.py, utils/prompts.py serves as the centralized prompt template loader, inline prompt constructor, and resilient response parsing engine for the codebase knowledge generation pipeline. It abstracts the retrieval of prompt files across varied architectural documentation modes (tutorial, advanced, api-reference, sdk), formats dynamic contextual payloads for downstream Large Language Model (LLM) calls, and transforms raw model outputs into structured, typed Python dictionaries. By decoupling prompt formatting and deserialization from workflow execution nodes, the module standardizes communication boundaries and shields downstream components from provider-specific generation quirks.

A central responsibility of the module is robust, fault-tolerant parsing of non-deterministic LLM completions. Generative language models frequently introduce syntax errors into YAML payloads, such as unquoted indicator characters (@, #, *), bare scalar quotes containing colons, invalid backtick wrapping around YAML keys, or premature response truncation caused by generation token ceilings. To prevent catastrophic pipeline failures during multi-stage indexing runs, utils/prompts.py implements a multi-tiered recovery architecture. It sequentially attempts standard deserialization, regex-driven indicator quoting, scalar-to-block conversion (|-), top-level key segmentation, and granular line-by-line item salvaging, tracking unparsed artifacts to preserve factual claims without aborting entire batch jobs.

The following diagram illustrates the resilient response parsing workflow across both fact extraction and module grouping completions:

flowchart TD startInput["Incoming LLM Response"] --> checkTruncated{"Is Truncated?"} checkTruncated -->|Yes| errTruncated["Raise ValueError (Truncated)"] checkTruncated -->|No| checkFence{"Matches YAML Fence?"} checkFence -->|No| errNoFence["Raise ValueError (No YAML)"] checkFence -->|Yes| extractYAML["Extract and Normalize YAML Content"] subgraph SubgraphFactsRecovery["Facts Parsing Pipeline"] entryFacts["_quote_indicator_values"] --> tryBaseLoad{"Attempt yaml.BaseLoader"} tryBaseLoad -->|Success| validateData{"Contains Required Keys?"} tryBaseLoad -->|Fail| applyBlockQuotes["_block_quotes Conversion"] applyBlockQuotes --> tryReLoad{"Attempt Second BaseLoader"} tryReLoad -->|Success| validateData tryReLoad -->|Fail| salvageLists["_salvage_yaml_lists (Per-Chunk / Per-Item)"] salvageLists --> validateData validateData -->|No| errInvalid["Raise ValueError (Missing Keys)"] validateData -->|Yes| returnFactsDict["Return Structured Facts Dict"] end subgraph SubgraphGroupingRecovery["Grouping Parsing Pipeline"] entryGrouping["parse_yaml_response"] --> tryStandard{"Standard yaml.safe_load"} tryStandard -->|Success| returnGroupDict["Return Grouping Dict"] tryStandard -->|Fail| unwrapRoles["Unwrap Backticked Roles"] unwrapRoles --> splitChunks["Split on Top-Level Section Headers"] splitChunks --> loadChunks["yaml.safe_load Per Chunk"] loadChunks --> verifySections{"Sections List Present?"} verifySections -->|Yes| returnGroupDict verifySections -->|No| errNoSections["Raise ValueError (No Sections)"] end extractYAML --> entryFacts extractYAML --> entryGrouping classDef entryNode stroke:#d33,stroke-width:3px,fill:#fff5f5; class startInput entryNode; class entryFacts entryNode; class entryGrouping entryNode; Hold "Alt" / "Option" to enable pan & zoom

docs.title: parse_file_index()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_file_index(idx_value):

Description: Extracts the first integer encountered from an LLM-returned file index value. It accommodates various scalar representations returned by models, including raw integers, annotated file path strings, and hyphenated numeric ranges, returning the leading integer component while delegating full range expansion to other utilities.

Parameters:

  • idx_value (Any): The raw input value representing a file index, typically an int, str, or composite string.

Returns:

  • int | None: The first parsed integer extracted from the string representation of the argument, or None if no numeric digits are found.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions. Non-numeric or empty string conversions safely evaluate to None.

Example:

def parse_file_index(idx_value):
    nums = re.findall(r"\d+", str(idx_value))
    return int(nums[0]) if nums else None

The function executes a regular expression search over the string cast of idx_value, isolating all contiguous sequences of ASCII digits. If the match list is populated, the first element is converted to a native Python int and returned immediately. This design provides basic tolerance for models that return prose annotations alongside numeric IDs (such as "3 # path/to/file.py"), though it truncates hyphenated ranges to their starting index without evaluating downstream boundaries.

docs.title: parse_file_indices()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_file_indices(idx_value) -> list[int]:

Description: Strictly parses an index representation returned by an LLM into an explicit list of integer indices. Unlike parse_file_index(), this function discriminates between explicit file indices, annotated numeric comments, and expanded ascending index ranges, actively rejecting file paths containing digits or arbitrary prose to avoid linking hallucinated files.

docs.title: Phase 1: Primitive Type Guarding
docs.text:
if isinstance(idx_value, bool):
        return []
    if isinstance(idx_value, int):
        return [idx_value] if idx_value >= 0 else []
    text = str(idx_value) if isinstance(idx_value, str) else ""

The initial phase screens against primitive Python types to prevent standard type coercion errors. Booleans are rejected outright because Python treats bool as a subclass of int (which would otherwise evaluate True to index 1). Non-negative integers are packaged directly into single-element lists, while negative integers are discarded to avoid negative indexing bugs. Non-string inputs are converted to empty strings to guarantee that subsequent regular expression operations execute against clean character sequences.

docs.title: Phase 2: Single Index Matching
docs.text:
single = _INDEX_RE.match(text)
    if single:
        return [int(single.group(1))]

The second phase evaluates the input string against _INDEX_RE. This regular expression matches single non-negative integers bounded by whitespace and optionally followed by a hash comment (#) containing trailing file path metadata. If a match occurs, the isolated integer token from capture group 1 is parsed and returned as a single-item list. This pattern ensures annotated tokens like "3 # utils/prompts.py" resolve strictly to [3] without executing arbitrary range scans.

docs.title: Phase 3: Range and Span Expansion
docs.text:
span = _INDEX_RANGE_RE.match(text)
    if span and int(span.group(1)) <= int(span.group(2)) and int(span.group(2)) - int(span.group(1)) < 10000:
        return list(range(int(span.group(1)), int(span.group(2)) + 1))
    return []

The final phase evaluates candidate ranges using _INDEX_RANGE_RE, matching ascending intervals separated by hyphens, double periods, en-dashes, or the word "to". To prevent Denial of Service (DoS) memory exhaustion from maliciously crafted or hallucinated LLM responses, the lower boundary must be less than or equal to the upper boundary, and the total span difference must be strictly under 10,000 items. If these validation constraints pass, the inclusive range is expanded into a Python list[int]; otherwise, an empty list is returned to signal an unparseable entry.

docs.title: load_prompt_template()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def load_prompt_template(template_name, advanced_mode=False, mode=None):

Description: Reads and returns the raw Markdown prompt template from the project's prompts/ directory tree. It resolves template directory hierarchies dynamically based on operating mode configurations and records file retrieval telemetry to the debug log destination.

Parameters:

  • template_name (str): The base filename of the template, excluding the .md extension (e.g., "extract_facts").
  • advanced_mode (bool, default: False): Fallback flag toggling between "advanced" and "tutorial" template directories when mode is unspecified.
  • mode (str | None, default: None): Explicit operating mode subdirectory (e.g., "api-reference", "sdk", "common"). Overrides advanced_mode if provided.

Returns:

  • str: The complete decoded text contents of the prompt template file.

Raises:

  • FileNotFoundError: If the constructed prompt template file path does not exist on disk.
  • OSError: If the file cannot be accessed or read due to filesystem permission constraints.

Example:

def load_prompt_template(template_name, advanced_mode=False, mode=None):
    if mode is None:
        prompt_dir = "advanced" if advanced_mode else "tutorial"
    else:
        prompt_dir = mode

    path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))), "prompts", prompt_dir, f"{template_name}.md")
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        content = f.read()
    from utils.output import emit_raw

    emit_raw("DEBUG", f"load_prompt_template | loaded '{template_name}.md' from prompts/{prompt_dir}/", dest="LOG")
    return content

The function computes an absolute path to the target Markdown file by traversing up two directory levels from the current script location to locate the repository root. The file is ingested using utf-8-sig encoding, ensuring that any leading Byte Order Marks (BOM) are stripped cleanly without corrupting prompt preambles. To avoid circular import cycles during early application bootstrapping, it lazily imports emit_raw from utils.output within local function scope, dispatching a debug telemetry log before returning the string content.

docs.title: parse_yaml_response()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_yaml_response(response):

Description: Extracts and deserializes raw YAML payloads contained within Markdown code fences from an LLM completion string. It validates that the completion was not prematurely terminated by token context limits prior to invoking PyYAML.

Parameters:

  • response (str | Any): The text response returned by the LLM, or a response object implementing a truncated boolean attribute.

Returns:

  • Any: The deserialized Python data structure (typically a dict or list) parsed from the YAML block.

Raises:

  • ValueError: Raised if the response object has its truncated attribute set to True, if the response does not contain matching ```yaml fences, or if PyYAML fails to parse the extracted block.

Example:

def parse_yaml_response(response):
    if getattr(response, "truncated", False):
        raise ValueError("LLM response was truncated before the YAML block completed")
    try:
        yaml_str = response.strip().split("```yaml")[1].split("```")[0].strip()
        return yaml.safe_load(yaml_str)
    except Exception as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Failed to parse YAML: {e}") from e

The function first guards against truncated completions by inspecting getattr(response, "truncated", False). This prevents silent data loss where an LLM reaches an output token limit mid-generation, leaving a validly fenced prefix that omits subsequent structural elements. It isolates the YAML substring by splitting on the opening ```yaml marker and closing ``` delimiter. If delimiter extraction fails or if yaml.safe_load encounters malformed syntax, the original error is wrapped and re-raised as a descriptive ValueError.

docs.title: parse_grouping_response()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_grouping_response(response):

Description: Parses the multi-section YAML reply generated by the group_modules.md prompt. It handles structural errors introduced by language models, such as wrapping YAML key values in Markdown backticks or producing invalid document boundaries, by executing top-level chunked recovery across section headers.

docs.title: Phase 1: Direct YAML Deserialization
docs.text:
try:
        return parse_yaml_response(response)
    except ValueError:
        if getattr(response, "truncated", False) or "```yaml" not in response:
            raise

The function initially attempts an optimistic parse via parse_yaml_response(). If this succeeds without syntax errors, the parsed dictionary is returned immediately. If a ValueError is raised, the function checks whether the response was explicitly truncated or entirely lacks a ```yaml fence; if either condition is true, recovery is impossible, and the exception is propagated immediately to trigger downstream node retries.

docs.title: Phase 2: Syntax Normalization and Chunk Recovery
docs.text:
yaml_str = response.split("```yaml", 1)[1].split("```", 1)[0]
        yaml_str = re.sub(r"(?m)^(\s*(?:-\s+)?role\s*:\s*)`([^`\n]*)`", r"\1\2", yaml_str)
        parsed = {}
        for chunk in re.split(r"(?m)^(?=(?:sections|dependencies)\s*:)", yaml_str):
            try:
                part = yaml.safe_load(chunk)
            except Exception:
                continue
            if isinstance(part, dict):
                parsed.update(part)
        if not isinstance(parsed.get("sections"), list):
            raise ValueError("Failed to parse YAML: no sections list in the grouping reply") from None
        return parsed

When standard parsing fails, the recovery phase isolates the YAML payload and applies regex normalization to unwrap backticks from around role: specifications (e.g., - role:core` becomes- role: core). It then splits the document on top-level section boundaries (sections:,descriptions:,dependencies:) using lookahead regex matching. Each chunk is parsed independently viayaml.safe_load(), allowing a syntax error inside one component (such as an unescaped character in a description) to be discarded without invalidating the navigation sidebar or dependency linkages. If the recovered dictionary fails to contain a validsectionslist, aValueError` is raised.

docs.title: build_verified_facts_block()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_verified_facts_block(facts: dict | None, doc_paths: dict) -> str:

Description: Constructs the {verified_facts} Markdown prompt context block used during API reference chapter drafting (draft_chapters.md). It aggregates verified AST declarations, cross-module import paths, configuration parameters, and raised error classes into an authoritative reference block that instructs the model to adhere strictly to verified source facts.

docs.title: Phase 1: Claims Validation and Target Filtering
docs.text:
if not facts or facts.get("claims") is None:
        return ""
    symbols = facts.get("symbols") or []
    modules = list(dict.fromkeys(edge["module"] for edge in facts.get("depends_on") or []))
    config = facts.get("config") or []
    errors = list(dict.fromkeys(item["name"] for item in facts.get("errors") or [] if item.get("role", "raised") != "caught"))
    if not (symbols or modules or config or errors):
        return ""

The function inspects the input facts dictionary, returning an empty string immediately if the dictionary is missing, if claims is None (signaling failed extraction), or if all fact categories are empty. It deduplicates imported dependency targets while preserving encounter order using dict.fromkeys(). For error structures, it filters out purely caught exceptions, retaining only exceptions explicitly raised or defined by the module to ensure the prompt accurately depicts the component's error-throwing contracts.

docs.title: Phase 2: Markdown Section Assembly
docs.text:
lines = ["VERIFIED FACTS OF THIS FILE (extracted from it and checked against its source code):"]
    if symbols:
        lines.append(
            "Symbols — document every one; copy each signature as written here (one marked 'start of the declaration' continues in the source: copy it in full from there):"
        )
        for symbol in symbols:
            owner = f"{symbol['parent']}." if symbol.get("parent") else ""
            visibility = f", {symbol['visibility']}" if symbol.get("visibility") else ""
            signature, partial = _fact_signature(symbol)
            marker = " — start of the declaration" if partial else ""
            lines.append(
                f"- {symbol.get('kind') or 'symbol'} {owner}{symbol['name']}{visibility} (line {symbol['line']}): {_code_span(signature)}{marker}"
            )
    if modules:
        lines.append("Project files this file imports — See Also must link each of them:")
        lines.extend(f"- {module} (doc: {doc_paths.get(module, module + '.md')})" for module in modules)
    if config:
        lines.append("Configuration it reads: " + ", ".join(f"{item['name']} ({item.get('kind') or 'config'})" for item in config))
    if errors:
        lines.append("Errors it raises or defines: " + ", ".join(errors))
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"

The second phase compiles the filtered categories into formatted Markdown bullet points. Each symbol entry formats its parent ownership, access visibility, source line, and signature string wrapped in backtick fences via _code_span(). Truncated or multi-line signatures are flagged with " — start of the declaration" to mandate that the model copy full definitions from the source code. Imported modules are annotated with their destination chapter paths via doc_paths, and configuration items and error classes are listed as comma-delimited summaries.

docs.title: build_facts_focus_note()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_facts_focus_note(lines: list[tuple[int, str]], limit: int = FACTS_FOCUS_LIMIT) -> str:

Description: Generates the {focus_note} prompt segment for follow-up AST extraction passes (extract_facts.md). When an initial extraction pass fails to account for lines that resemble declarations or imports, this function constructs targeted prompt instructions that constrain the LLM to analyze only the specified unverified line numbers.

Parameters:

  • lines (list[tuple[int, str]]): A list of tuples, each pairing a 1-based source line number with its corresponding raw text string.
  • limit (int, default: FACTS_FOCUS_LIMIT = 60): The maximum number of physical code lines to render directly inside the prompt note.

Returns:

  • str: The formatted follow-up instruction string containing enumerated line previews and remaining count warnings.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions.

Example:

def build_facts_focus_note(lines: list[tuple[int, str]], limit: int = FACTS_FOCUS_LIMIT) -> str:
    def shown_line(text: str) -> str:
        text = text.strip()
        return text if len(text) <= _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS else text[: _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS - 3] + "..."

    shown = "\n".join(f"  {number}: {shown_line(text)}" for number, text in lines[:limit])
    more = f"\n  ... and {len(lines) - limit} more such lines" if len(lines) > limit else ""
    return (
        "FOLLOW-UP: a first pass over this file reported nothing for the lines below, which look like declarations "
        "or imports. Report ONLY the facts on these lines, with the same four lists and rules; a line that is not a "
        "declaration a reader looks up (a local variable, a statement) gets nothing.\n"
        f"Lines:\n{shown}{more}\n"
    )

The function defines an internal helper, shown_line(), which strips leading and trailing whitespace and truncates lines exceeding _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS (200 characters) with an ellipsis (...). It slices the incoming line list up to limit entries, formatting each line with two-space indentation and its physical line number. If the total unverified line count exceeds the limit, a summary line is appended noting the remaining quantity. The assembled string establishes strict boundaries that instruct the LLM not to report local variables or procedural statements.

docs.title: parse_facts_response()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_facts_response(response, keys: tuple = FACTS_KEYS) -> dict:

Description: Parses the YAML completion from extract_facts.md or extract_manifest.md into a structured dictionary containing symbol lists, dependencies, configurations, and errors. It implements a multi-pass parsing and salvage routine that recovers valid declarations from syntactically malformed model responses while recording the count of unparseable items.

docs.title: Phase 1: Truncation Check and Fence Extraction
docs.text:
if getattr(response, "truncated", False):
        raise ValueError("LLM response was truncated before the YAML block completed")
    match = _FACTS_BLOCK_RE.search(response) or _FACTS_OPEN_RE.search(response)
    if not match:
        raise ValueError("Failed to parse YAML: no ```yaml block in the facts reply")
    indent = match.group(1)
    yaml_str = _quote_indicator_values("\n".join(line.removeprefix(indent) for line in match.group(2).split("\n")))
    unparsed = 0

The parsing pipeline begins by asserting that the response was not cut off by context boundaries via the truncated attribute check. It then searches for Markdown code blocks using _FACTS_BLOCK_RE (matching closed fences at uniform indentation) or _FACTS_OPEN_RE (matching unclosed fences reaching EOF). The common indentation prefix of the fence is stripped from all lines, and name-like fields containing YAML indicators are double-quoted via _quote_indicator_values() to prevent PyYAML parser exceptions on characters like @ or *.

docs.title: Phase 2: Indicator Quoting and Multi-Tier Parsing
docs.text:
try:
        data = _load_strings(yaml_str)
    except Exception:
        try:
            data = _load_strings(_block_quotes(yaml_str))
        except Exception:
            data, unparsed = _salvage_yaml_lists(_block_quotes(yaml_str), keys)
    if not isinstance(data, dict) or not any(key in data for key in keys):
        raise ValueError("Failed to parse YAML: no fact lists in the facts reply")

The second phase employs three tiered parsing attempts. First, it attempts a direct string load using _load_strings() (which utilizes yaml.BaseLoader to retain all scalars as strings). If this fails due to plain scalars containing syntax-breaking colons or quotes, it transforms single-line quotes into block scalars via _block_quotes() and retries _load_strings(). If the re-parse fails again, execution falls back to _salvage_yaml_lists(), which isolates individual list chunks and parses item-by-item to salvage valid records while counting lost entries.

docs.title: Phase 3: Dict Key Assembly and Lost Item Accounting
docs.text:
result = {}
    for key in keys:
        items = data.get(key)
        items = items if isinstance(items, list) else []
        result[key] = [item for item in items if isinstance(item, dict)]
        unparsed += len(items) - len(result[key])
    result["unparsed"] = unparsed
    return result

In the final phase, the parsed object is verified to contain at least one expected category key. The function iterates across the requested keys tuple (defaulting to FACTS_KEYS), ensuring that missing or null fields normalize to empty Python lists. It filters each list to keep only dictionary mappings, adding any non-mapping items (such as bare strings resulting from YAML formatting errors) to the running unparsed counter. The aggregated unparsed total is injected into the returned dictionary under the "unparsed" key.

docs.title: build_code_file_filter_prompt()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_code_file_filter_prompt(project_name: str, file_listing: str) -> str:

Description: Constructs the classification prompt for the DeterministicFileMapper workflow node. The prompt instructs an LLM to evaluate a repository file listing and bifurcate files into functional source code modules (containing APIs, classes, or logic) versus project build manifests (such as package.json, Cargo.toml, or pom.xml), while explicitly ignoring static assets, UI templates, and documentation.

Parameters:

  • project_name (str): The name or identifier of the target codebase.
  • file_listing (str): An indexed string representation of all discovered files across the repository, typically generated by build_directory_tree().

Returns:

  • str: The complete prompt string containing filtering criteria, exclusion rules, manifest guidelines, and target YAML output schemas.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions.

Example:

def build_code_file_filter_prompt(project_name: str, file_listing: str) -> str:
    return (
        f"For the project `{project_name}`, here is the list of all files in the codebase:

"
        f"{file_listing}

"
        f"Your task is to identify WHICH of these files are ACTUAL CODE files that contain "
        f"APIs, functions, classes, or core business logic.
"
        f"EXCLUDE: UI layouts (like .xaml, .storyboard, .html), configuration files "
        f"(like .xml, .json, .manifest, .ini), static assets, build scripts "
        f"(like .csproj, .sln), and documentation.

"
        f"Separately, list the MANIFESTS among the other files: files that declare a package, module, crate or "
        f"workspace name, or import path aliases, for this project's own code (for example package.json, "
        f"tsconfig.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, setup.cfg, composer.json, pom.xml, build.gradle, "
        f"*.csproj, mix.exs, pubspec.yaml, *.gemspec).

"
        f"Return ONLY YAML with the file indices of both lists:

"
        f"```yaml
code:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 3
manifests:
  - 2
```"
    )

The prompt construction embeds the repository name and formatted file tree into a structured directive. It enforces deterministic filtering by providing concrete file extension exclusion examples (.xaml, .xml, .json, .html) and comprehensive manifest patterns across polyglot ecosystems (Rust Cargo.toml, Go go.mod, Python pyproject.toml, Java pom.xml, etc.). The prompt mandates that the model respond strictly using YAML fenced blocks containing index integers under code and manifests keys.

docs.title: build_chapter_summary_prompt()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_chapter_summary_prompt(chapter_num: int, abstraction_name: str, chapter_content: str, language: str = "english") -> str:

Description: Constructs the prompt for generating a structured, four-dimension technical summary of a newly drafted chapter. This summary is injected into subsequent chapter drafting prompts to maintain narrative coherence, dependency context, and architectural consistency across the generated documentation suite.

Parameters:

  • chapter_num (int): The numeric sequence index of the chapter.
  • abstraction_name (str): The title or architectural abstraction represented by the chapter.
  • chapter_content (str): The full Markdown text of the generated chapter.
  • language (str, default: "english"): Target language for the summary generation.

Returns:

  • str: The complete prompt requesting a four-point technical brief.

Raises:

  • Does not raise exceptions.

Example:

def build_chapter_summary_prompt(chapter_num: int, abstraction_name: str, chapter_content: str, language: str = "english") -> str:
    lang_instruction = f"Write the entire summary in {language.capitalize()}. " if language.lower() != "english" else ""
    return (
        f"{lang_instruction}"
        f"Summarize the following documentation chapter as a structured technical brief. "
        f"For EACH of the 4 points below, write 3-5 concise technical sentences:\n\n"
        f"(1) **Component Scope & Responsibility**: What is the main technical domain this "
        f"chapter covers? What problems does it solve and what role does it play in the system?\n\n"
        f"(2) **Key Technical Elements**: What are the specific classes, services, functions, "
        f"data models, or protocols discussed? Name them and describe their concrete roles.\n\n"
        f"(3) **Implementation Patterns & Architecture**: What design patterns, communication "
        f"protocols, data flow strategies, error handling mechanisms, or security measures "
        f"are covered? How are they implemented?\n\n"
        f"(4) **System Integration & Dependencies**: How does this component interface with "
        f"other parts of the system? What does it consume from or provide to other components? "
        f"What are the key integration points?\n\n"
        f"---\n"
        f"Chapter {chapter_num}: {abstraction_name}\n"
        f"{chapter_content}"
    )

The function conditionally prepends a localization instruction when language is not English. It structures the summary request around four analytical dimensions: scope, key technical symbols, implementation patterns, and system integration. By enforcing a constraint of 3-5 concise technical sentences per dimension, the generated summary retains a compact token footprint while capturing architectural context for downstream prompts.

docs.title: FACTS_KEYS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: FACTS_KEYS = ("symbols", "dependencies", "config", "errors")

Description: A 4-element tuple of strings defining the canonical top-level keys expected in an AST fact extraction completion. Used as the default validation boundary in parse_facts_response().

docs.title: FACTS_FOCUS_LIMIT
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: FACTS_FOCUS_LIMIT = 60

Description: An integer constant defining the maximum number of unverified code lines displayed in the follow-up note constructed by build_facts_focus_note(). Prevents context window saturation during iterative extraction loops.

docs.title: _fact_signature()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _fact_signature(symbol: dict) -> tuple[str, bool]:

Description: Normalizes and truncates a verified symbol signature string for safe inclusion in prompt Markdown code spans. It strips leading decorators or compiler attributes, squashes multi-line declarations into a single space-delimited string, checks for bracket balance, and clamps string length against _FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS.

Parameters:

  • symbol (dict): A symbol fact mapping extracted from the codebase, containing "signature", "truncated", and name fields.

Returns:

  • tuple[str, bool]: A 2-tuple containing:
    1. The sanitized, single-line signature text (appended with an ellipsis " …" if partial).
    2. A boolean indicating whether the signature was cut short or requires full source verification.

Example:

def _fact_signature(symbol: dict) -> tuple[str, bool]:
    lines = str(symbol.get("signature", "")).split("\n")
    while len(lines) > 1 and re.match(r"\s*(?:@|#\[|\[[A-Z])", lines[0]):
        lines = lines[1:]
    text = " ".join(" ".join(lines).split())
    code = re.sub(r"\"(?:\\.|[^\"\\])*\"|'(?:\\.|[^'\\])*'", "", text)
    partial = bool(symbol.get("truncated")) or code.count("(") > code.count(")") or code.count("[") > code.count("]")
    if len(text) > _FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS:
        text, partial = text[:_FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS].rstrip(), True
    return (text + " …" if partial else text), partial

The function splits the signature on newlines and drops leading lines starting with decorators or attribute annotations (@property, #[inline], [Obsolete]). It squashes all internal whitespace runs into single spaces. To determine if the signature represents an incomplete fragment, it strips string literals (to avoid counting characters inside quotes) and tests whether opening parentheses or brackets exceed closing ones. Finally, if the line exceeds 200 characters (_FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS), it is sliced and marked as partial.

docs.title: _code_span()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _code_span(text: str) -> str:

Description: Wraps a code snippet in an inline Markdown backtick span designed so that internal backtick characters cannot accidentally close the span.

Parameters:

  • text (str): The raw code or signature text to encapsulate.

Returns:

  • str: The backtick-wrapped Markdown code span, padded with spaces if internal backticks exist.

Example:

def _code_span(text: str) -> str:
    fence = "`" * (max((len(run) for run in re.findall(r"`+", text)), default=0) + 1)
    return f"{fence} {text} {fence}" if "`" in text else f"{fence}{text}{fence}"

The function inspects text for all contiguous sequences of backtick characters (```). It generates an enclosing delimiter sequence whose length is strictly one character longer than the longest backtick run found inside the text (defaulting to a single backtick if none exist). If the text contains any backticks, CommonMark rules mandate space padding adjacent to the boundary fences to prevent parser collisions; otherwise, it formats the fence flush against the string.

docs.title: _load_strings()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _load_strings(text: str):

Description: Deserializes a YAML string while forcing all scalar primitives to remain native Python strings. Prevents unintended type coercion of values like HTTP status codes (404), boolean literals (on, no), or software version strings (3.10).

Parameters:

  • text (str): The raw YAML string to load.

Returns:

  • Any: A data structure where all primitive values are typed as str, list, or dict.

Example:

def _load_strings(text: str):
    return yaml.load(text, Loader=yaml.BaseLoader)

The function invokes yaml.load() using PyYAML's yaml.BaseLoader. Unlike yaml.SafeLoader or yaml.FullLoader, BaseLoader skips standard type resolvers, meaning numbers, dates, booleans, and nulls are ingested without transformation as string objects. This protects symbol names, configuration values, and module identifiers from corruption during AST parsing.

docs.title: _quote_indicator_values()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _quote_indicator_values(text: str) -> str:

Description: Wraps name-like YAML values that begin with special indicator characters inside double quotes. Eliminates syntax errors caused by symbols like @decorator, #channel, or *args.

Parameters:

  • text (str): The YAML document text to sanitize.

Returns:

  • str: The sanitized YAML string with offending indicator-prefixed values escaped and enclosed in double quotes.

Example:

def _quote_indicator_values(text: str) -> str:
    return _INDICATOR_VALUE_RE.sub(lambda m: m[1] + '"' + m[2].replace("\\", "\\\\").replace('"', '\\"') + '"', text)

The function uses _INDICATOR_VALUE_RE to scan for dictionary keys like name:, entry:, alias:, or target: followed by tokens starting with indicator characters (@, ,, #, *, &, !, %). The substitution callback preserves the key indentation while escaping backslashes and quotes within the value string, enclosing the result in double quotes. This allows values like name: @acme/core or name: *args to pass PyYAML tokenization without being misconstrued as YAML anchors or invalid syntax.

docs.title: _block_quotes()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _block_quotes(text: str) -> str:

Description: Converts plain single-line signature: and evidence: scalar entries into YAML literal block scalars (|-). Resolves parsing errors caused by source code quotes that contain colons, hash symbols, or unbalanced quotes.

Parameters:

  • text (str): The YAML text containing candidate scalar lines.

Returns:

  • str: The transformed YAML text where bare code quotes are rewritten into indented block scalars.

Example:

def _block_quotes(text: str) -> str:
    return _PLAIN_QUOTE_RE.sub(lambda m: m[0] if _WHOLE_SCALAR_RE.match(m[3]) else f"{m[1]}{m[2]}: |-\n{' ' * (len(m[1]) + 2)}{m[3]}", text)

The function evaluates lines matching _PLAIN_QUOTE_RE. If the value after signature: or evidence: already constitutes a valid quoted string or block indicator (verified via _WHOLE_SCALAR_RE), it is left unchanged. Otherwise, it rewrites the line to introduce a |- literal block indicator (which strips trailing newlines) and shifts the code quote to a new line indented two spaces deeper than the parent key. This prevents internal colons (e.g., def run(self):) from prematurely terminating scalar parsing.

docs.title: _salvage_yaml_lists()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: def _salvage_yaml_lists(yaml_str: str, keys: tuple) -> tuple[dict, int]:

Description: Granular recovery parser that salvages valid entries from a broken YAML document. It isolates each top-level key list independently, and if a list still fails to parse, breaks it into individual list items based on indentation to recover all valid dictionaries while accounting for lost items.

docs.title: Phase 1: Chunk Identification by Key Header
docs.text:
names = "|".join(keys)
    parsed, lost = {}, 0
    for chunk in re.split(rf"(?m)^(?=(?:{names})\s*:)", yaml_str):
        head = re.match(rf"({names})\s*:", chunk)
        if not head:
            continue
        try:
            part = _load_strings(chunk)
        except Exception:
            part = None
        if isinstance(part, dict):
            parsed.update(part)
            continue

The function constructs a dynamic regex from the requested category keys (e.g., "symbols|dependencies|config|errors"), splitting the document on lines where those keys begin. For each isolated section chunk, it extracts the key header and attempts to parse the chunk in isolation using _load_strings(). If the chunk parses cleanly as a dictionary, its contents are merged into parsed and the loop advances to the next section without item-level decomposition.

docs.title: Phase 2: Item-by-Item Indentation Extraction
docs.text:
body = chunk[head.end() :]
        first = re.search(r"(?m)^([ \t]*)- ", body)
        if not first:
            continue
        indent = first.group(1)
        items = []
        for piece in re.split(rf"(?m)^(?={re.escape(indent)}- )", body):
            if not piece.startswith(f"{indent}- "):
                continue
            text = "\n".join(line.removeprefix(indent) for line in piece.split("\n"))
            try:
                item = _load_strings(text)
            except Exception:
                lost += 1
                continue
            if isinstance(item, list) and item and isinstance(item[0], dict):
                items.append(item[0])
            else:
                lost += 1
        parsed[head.group(1)] = items
    return parsed, lost

When an entire list section fails to parse, the function isolates the list body and identifies the indentation of its first list item delimiter (-). It then splits the body into individual item pieces using a lookahead on that exact indentation pattern. Each item is stripped of its relative indentation prefix and parsed independently via _load_strings(). Successfully parsed dictionary items are collected into the items list; any item that throws an exception or fails to deserialize as a dictionary increments the lost counter. The recovered items are stored under their respective top-level key.

docs.title: Internal Regular Expression Constants
docs.text:
The module defines compiled regular expressions to support its parsing and transformation subroutines:

Constant Pattern / Definition Purpose _INDEX_RE re.compile(r"^\s*(\d+)\s*(?:#.*)?$") Matches single integers optionally followed by hash comments (e.g., "3 # file.py"). _INDEX_RANGE_RE re.compile(r"^\s*(\d+)\s*(?:-|\.\.\|–\|to)\s*(\d+)\s*(?:#.*)?$") Matches ascending ranges using hyphens, dots, en-dashes, or "to" (e.g., "0-3", "4..7"). _FACTS_BLOCK_RE re.compile(r"(?msi)^([ ]*)```ya?ml[^ ]* (.*?)^\1```[ ]*$") Matches closed YAML blocks where opening and closing fences share identical indentation. _FACTS_OPEN_RE re.compile(r"(?msi)^([ ]*)```ya?ml[^ ]* (.*)") Matches unclosed YAML blocks reaching the end of the completion text. _PLAIN_QUOTE_RE re.compile(r"(?m)^([ ]*(?:- )?)(signature\|evidence):[ ]+(\S.*)$") Matches unescaped scalar code quotes under signature: or evidence: keys. _WHOLE_SCALAR_RE re.compile(r"""^(?:"(?:\.\|[^"\])*"\|'(?:''\|[^'])*'\|[\|>][-+0-9]*)[ ]*(?:#.*)?$""") Identifies valid quoted scalars or block indicators that do not require block scalar wrapping. _INDICATOR_VALUE_RE re.compile(r"(?m)^([ ]*(?:- )?(?:name\|entry\|alias\|target\|base\|parent):[ ]+)([@#&!%]\S||>\S)(?:[ ]+#.)?$")` Matches name-like fields whose values begin with YAML indicator symbols. _FACT_SIGNATURE_CHARS 200 Maximum character length allocated for verified signatures in prompt blocks before truncation. _FOCUS_LINE_CHARS 200 Maximum character width rendered for individual code lines inside the facts focus note.

docs.title: Facts Response Structure
docs.text:
The dictionary returned by parse_facts_response() adheres to the following structural schema:

Key Type Description symbols list[dict[str, Any]] List of extracted symbol mappings (functions, classes, methods). dependencies list[dict[str, Any]] List of imported module specifiers and external package references. config list[dict[str, Any]] List of configuration values, environment variables, or flags read by the module. errors list[dict[str, Any]] List of exception classes raised, caught, or defined within the source file. unparsed int Count of list items that could not be parsed or were discarded due to formatting errors.

Example dictionary returned by parse_facts_response():

{
    "symbols": [
        {
            "name": "parse_file_index",
            "kind": "function",
            "line": "16",
            "signature": "def parse_file_index(idx_value):"
        }
    ],
    "dependencies": [
        {
            "module": "utils.output",
            "evidence": "from utils.output import emit_raw"
        }
    ],
    "config": [],
    "errors": [
        {
            "name": "ValueError",
            "role": "raised"
        }
    ],
    "unparsed": 0
}

docs.title: Grouping Response Structure
docs.text:
The dictionary returned by parse_grouping_response() satisfies the following structural schema:

Key Type Description sections list[dict[str, Any]] Hierarchical list of navigation sections grouping modules by role. descriptions dict[str, str] (optional) Mapping of module or section identifiers to high-level architectural descriptions. dependencies list[dict[str, Any]] (optional) Architectural dependency edges established between modules or layers.

docs.title: Verified Facts Input Schema
docs.text:
The facts dictionary supplied to build_verified_facts_block() expects the following structure:

Field Type Description claims Any Verification sentinel; if None, the function considers extraction to have failed. symbols list[dict[str, Any]] List of verified symbol records extracted from source code. depends_on list[dict[str, str]] List of dependency records with a "module" key naming imported files. config list[dict[str, str]] List of verified configuration mappings with "name" and optional "kind" keys. errors list[dict[str, str]] List of error mappings containing "name" and "role" ("raised", "caught").

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The module relies primarily on ValueError to report parsing and structural anomalies, avoiding custom exception hierarchies. Errors are surfaced under specific conditions:

  • Truncation Rejection: In both parse_yaml_response() and parse_facts_response(), incoming response objects are inspected for the attribute truncated. If getattr(response, "truncated", False) evaluates to True, a ValueError is raised immediately. This prevents incomplete YAML documents from being partially parsed, which would silently drop declarations or section links.
  • Missing YAML Fences: When parse_yaml_response() or parse_facts_response() cannot identify an opening ```yaml or ```yml code fence, a ValueError is raised rather than falling back to guessing scalar boundaries.
  • Missing Required Keys: In parse_grouping_response(), if the recovered structure lacks a valid sections list, a ValueError is raised. Similarly, parse_facts_response() raises a ValueError if the output dictionary contains none of the requested category keys.
  • PyYAML Exception Wrapping: Unhandled parsing errors from yaml.safe_load are caught, contextualized, and re-raised using Python's from e exception chaining syntax to maintain debugging tracebacks.

docs.title: thinking.py
docs.text: Source: utils/thinking.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
utils/thinking.py serves as the reasoning effort orchestration and budget planning engine for the codebase knowledge generation pipeline. Large language model (LLM) providers expose disparate configuration interfaces for extended reasoning—Anthropic Claude utilizes discrete effort allocations (low, medium, high), Google Gemini relies on integer token budgets or model-specific level enumerations, and OpenRouter passes effort directives through catalog-defined metadata. This module abstracts these provider-specific reasoning protocols into a normalized, provider-neutral scale (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max) and maps distinct reasoning budgets to individual pipeline execution stages (referred to as "nodes").

The module computes a comprehensive execution plan (thinking_plan) mapping every LLM call site (NODE_KEYS) to a target thinking effort level. The resolution logic enforces a strict three-tier precedence hierarchy: explicit per-node command-line overrides (--thinking-override NODE=LEVEL) supersede a global pipeline-wide level setting (--thinking-level LEVEL), which in turn supersedes curated profile presets (--thinking-profile PROFILE). Preconfigured profiles (economy, balanced, quality, max) assign calibrated reasoning effort based on the computational complexity of each stage—allocating maximum reasoning to structural synthesis tasks (such as whole-codebase abstraction discovery and reduction) while constraining mechanical tasks (such as file classification or UI string translation) to minimal or low effort.

At runtime, downstream workflow nodes retrieve their assigned reasoning budget using resolve_thinking_level against the shared pipeline state. When dispatching inference requests, provider-specific adapters invoke clamp_level to project the normalized project level onto the subset of levels natively supported by the target LLM. If a requested effort level is unsupported by a model, clamp_level deterministically selects the nearest available tier along the ordinal effort scale, resolving equidistant ties toward lower computational effort to prevent unexpected cost inflation.

flowchart TD subgraph InputResolution["Input Parsing and Profile Resolution"] rawProfile["CLI Profile / Provider Input"] --> resolveProfile["resolve_profile_name()"] rawOverrides["CLI Overrides (NODE=LEVEL)"] --> parseOverrides["parse_overrides()"] end subgraph PlanBuilding["Plan Synthesis Hierarchy"] checkGlobal{"Global Level Specified?"} resolveProfile --> checkGlobal checkGlobal -->|Yes| applyGlobal["Set All Nodes to Global Level"] checkGlobal -->|No| checkProfile{"Profile in Known Profiles?"} checkProfile -->|Yes| loadProfile["Load Base Profile Matrix"] checkProfile -->|No (off)| loadDefaults["Assign None (Model Defaults)"] loadProfile --> applyMode["Apply Mode Adjustments (_MODE_ADJUSTMENTS)"] applyGlobal --> applyOverrides["Merge Node Overrides"] loadDefaults --> applyOverrides applyMode --> applyOverrides applyOverrides --> finalPlan["Output thinking_plan Dictionary"] end subgraph RuntimeExecution["Runtime Resolution and Provider Clamping"] callSite["Workflow Node Execution"] --> resolveLevel["resolve_thinking_level(shared, node_key)"] resolveLevel --> targetLevel["Target Normalized Level"] targetLevel --> clampCheck{"Supported by Model?"} clampCheck -->|Yes| exactLevel["Apply Exact Level"] clampCheck -->|No| clampExec["clamp_level() Distance Calculation"] clampExec --> clampedLevel["Apply Nearest Supported Level (Ties to Lower)"] end InputResolution --> PlanBuilding PlanBuilding --> RuntimeExecution classDef entryNode stroke:#d33,stroke-width:3px,fill:#fff5f5; class rawProfile entryNode class checkGlobal entryNode class callSite entryNode Hold "Alt" / "Option" to enable pan & zoom

docs.title: THINKING_LEVELS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: THINKING_LEVELS = ("minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max")

Description: Immutable tuple defining the complete, ordered effort continuum supported across the system. Positions within the tuple dictate relative computational intensity, which clamp_level() utilizes to compute distance and resolve nearest-match substitutions. The minimal tier is reserved for select OpenRouter models and is omitted from standard project profiles.

# Definition in utils/thinking.py
THINKING_LEVELS = ("minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max")

The scale provides an ordinal foundation for distance comparisons. When algorithms compute metric distance between unsupported and supported model configurations, indices within THINKING_LEVELS establish the exact coordinate space.

docs.title: THINKING_PROFILES
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: THINKING_PROFILES = ("auto", "off", "economy", "balanced", "quality", "max")

Description: Immutable tuple listing valid configuration profile names accepted via the command-line interface. Profiles range from completely unmanaged model defaults (off), through cost-optimized tiers (economy, balanced, quality), up to unconstrained reasoning allocations (max).

# Definition in utils/thinking.py
THINKING_PROFILES = ("auto", "off", "economy", "balanced", "quality", "max")

The default profile auto dynamically resolves at startup to either balanced or off depending on the active provider's compatibility with per-model reasoning configurations.

docs.title: NODE_KEYS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: NODE_KEYS = ( "filter_files", "extract_facts", "map_abstractions", "reduce_abstractions", "identify_abstractions", "analyze_relationships", "order_chapters", "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "group_modules", "translate_strings", )

Description: Canonical tuple of all LLM call sites across all documentation pipeline modes, declared in execution pipeline order. Acts as the validation authority against which per-node overrides are checked.

# LLM call sites, in pipeline order.
NODE_KEYS = (
    "filter_files",  # DeterministicFileMapper — code/non-code file classification (api-reference)
    "extract_facts",  # ExtractFacts — per-file symbols, dependencies, config, errors with source quotes (api-reference)
    "map_abstractions",  # MapAbstractions — per-batch abstraction extraction (batch route)
    "reduce_abstractions",  # ReduceAbstractions — merge partial abstractions (batch route)
    "identify_abstractions",  # IdentifyAbstractions — whole-codebase abstraction discovery (direct route)
    "analyze_relationships",  # AnalyzeRelationships — project summary + abstraction relationships
    "order_chapters",  # OrderChapters — pedagogical chapter ordering
    "write_chapters",  # WriteChapters — long-form chapter / reference page generation
    "chapter_summary",  # WriteChapters — 3-5 sentence summary for cross-chapter context
    "group_modules",  # CombineTutorial — MkDocs nav grouping (api-reference, 6+ modules)
    "translate_strings",  # i18n — CLI string table translation (first run in a new language)
)

Every invocation of an LLM within the repository passes one of these identifiers to the centralized invocation layer. By declaring them in execution order, the system can systematically iterate through nodes when building default plans and formatting diagnostic startup outputs.

docs.title: MODE_NODES
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: MODE_NODES = { "tutorial": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"), "advanced": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"), "sdk": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"), "api-reference": ("filter_files", "extract_facts", "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "group_modules", "translate_strings"), }

Description: Mapping of documentation generation modes (tutorial, advanced, sdk, api-reference) to the specific sequence of node keys executed within that mode. Used to filter startup log outputs so that only active nodes are displayed to the operator.

# Nodes that can make an LLM call in each mode. api-reference always takes the deterministic
# route (1:1 file mapping) and is the only mode with MkDocs nav grouping.
_ANALYSIS_NODES = ("map_abstractions", "reduce_abstractions", "identify_abstractions", "analyze_relationships", "order_chapters")
MODE_NODES = {
    "tutorial": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"),
    "advanced": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"),
    "sdk": (*_ANALYSIS_NODES, "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "translate_strings"),
    "api-reference": ("filter_files", "extract_facts", "write_chapters", "chapter_summary", "group_modules", "translate_strings"),
}

The api-reference mode bypasses codebase-wide heuristic abstraction analysis (_ANALYSIS_NODES) in favor of deterministic file ingestion via filter_files and extract_facts. In contrast, narrative modes (tutorial, advanced, sdk) execute the full abstraction extraction and chapter ordering sequence.

docs.title: PROFILED_PROVIDERS
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: PROFILED_PROVIDERS = ("ANTHROPIC", "GEMINI", "OPENROUTER")

Description: Identifies inference providers whose contemporary models support granular per-request reasoning effort parameters. Used by resolve_profile_name() to decide whether the auto profile should activate managed thinking profiles or revert to vendor defaults.

# Providers whose thinking controls are mapped per model (auto → balanced).
PROFILED_PROVIDERS = ("ANTHROPIC", "GEMINI", "OPENROUTER")

For models under Anthropic, Google Gemini, and OpenRouter, reasoning effort serves as the primary cost and quality control lever. For generic endpoints (such as local Ollama instances or standard OpenAI-compatible gateways), thinking controls are unmapped by default.

docs.title: resolve_profile_name()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def resolve_profile_name(profile: str | None, provider: str | None) -> str:

Description: Resolves dynamic or omitted profile names into concrete profile identifiers. Specifically evaluates the auto profile keyword against the target LLM provider: providers listed in PROFILED_PROVIDERS receive the balanced profile, whereas all other providers fall back to off (deferring to native backend model defaults).

Parameters:

  • profile (str | None): The raw profile string supplied by user configuration or CLI arguments. Defaults to "auto" if None or empty.
  • provider (str | None): Canonical provider name (e.g., "ANTHROPIC", "GEMINI", "OPENROUTER", "OLLAMA").

Returns:

  • str: Resolved profile name ("balanced", "off", or the normalized lowercase profile string).

Raises:

  • None directly.

Example:

# Implementation from utils/thinking.py
def resolve_profile_name(profile: str | None, provider: str | None) -> str:
    """Resolve `auto` to a concrete profile for the active provider."""
    profile = (profile or "auto").lower()
    if profile == "auto":
        return "balanced" if provider in PROFILED_PROVIDERS else "off"
    return profile

The function guarantees safe string operations by forcing inputs to lowercase and providing "auto" as a fallback for missing values. When evaluated against modern providers capable of extended deliberation, it activates the balanced profile automatically. For uncalibrated or self-hosted backends where manual effort settings might cause payload validation rejections, it resolves to "off".

docs.title: clamp_level()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def clamp_level(level: str, supported) -> str | None:

Description: Maps a target normalized thinking level to the nearest level supported by a specific model backend. If the requested level is directly supported, it returns unchanged. If unsupported, the function filters THINKING_LEVELS to find all levels valid for the target model, measures the absolute distance in ordinal space, and selects the closest supported tier. In the event of an equidistant tie between higher and lower tiers, the algorithm selects the lower index to mitigate unexpected token consumption and cost.

Parameters:

  • level (str): Target thinking level name (e.g., "medium", "xhigh").
  • supported (Iterable[str]): Collection, set, or sequence of level names supported by the active model configuration.

Returns:

  • str | None: The exact level if supported; otherwise the nearest supported level on the THINKING_LEVELS scale. Returns None if the target level is not recognized or if supported contains no elements present on THINKING_LEVELS.

Raises:

  • None directly.

Example:

# Implementation from utils/thinking.py
def clamp_level(level: str, supported) -> str | None:
    """Return `level` if the model supports it, else the nearest supported level on
    THINKING_LEVELS (ties → lower). None when nothing on the scale is supported."""
    if level in supported:
        return level
    ranked = [lvl for lvl in THINKING_LEVELS if lvl in supported]
    if not ranked or level not in THINKING_LEVELS:
        return None
    target = THINKING_LEVELS.index(level)
    return min(ranked, key=lambda lvl: (abs(THINKING_LEVELS.index(lvl) - target), THINKING_LEVELS.index(lvl)))

The algorithm constructs ranked, a list preserving the canonical ordering of THINKING_LEVELS while filtering out unsupported levels. It computes target by locating level in THINKING_LEVELS. The min() evaluation uses a 2-tuple key: (abs(index - target), index). The primary sort key minimizes metric distance, while the secondary sort key breaks ties by choosing the smallest index (lower computational effort).

docs.title: parse_overrides()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def parse_overrides(values: list[str] | None) -> tuple[dict, list[str]]:

Description: Parses and validates raw command-line override arguments formatted as NODE=LEVEL. Strips whitespace, forces lowercase normalization, and verifies that the node identifier exists in NODE_KEYS and the level exists in THINKING_LEVELS. Returns a dictionary of valid overrides alongside a list of malformed or invalid declarations.

Parameters:

  • values (list[str] | None): List of string parameters passed via CLI arguments (e.g., ["write_chapters=high", "extract_facts=low"]).

Returns:

  • tuple[dict, list[str]]: A 2-tuple containing:
    1. overrides (dict[str, str]): Mapping of valid node keys to validated thinking level strings.
    2. invalid (list[str]): List of input strings that failed delimiter, node key, or level validation.

Raises:

  • None directly.

Example:

# Implementation from utils/thinking.py
def parse_overrides(values: list[str] | None) -> tuple[dict, list[str]]:
    """Parse NODE=LEVEL strings. Returns (overrides, invalid_values)."""
    overrides, invalid = {}, []
    for value in values or []:
        node, sep, level = value.partition("=")
        node, level = node.strip().lower(), level.strip().lower()
        if not sep or node not in NODE_KEYS or level not in THINKING_LEVELS:
            invalid.append(value)
        else:
            overrides[node] = level
    return overrides, invalid

The function utilizes str.partition("=") to separate key-value pairs without raising exceptions on missing delimiters. Inputs lacking an = separator, targeting unrecognized nodes, or referencing invalid effort names are accumulated into invalid for upstream reporting, while well-formed entries populate the overrides dictionary.

docs.title: build_thinking_plan()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def build_thinking_plan(profile: str, mode: str, global_level: str | None, overrides: dict) -> dict:

Description: Assembles the complete mapping of every node in NODE_KEYS to its resolved thinking level string or None. Implements the system's precedence model: explicit overrides take highest precedence; global levels take secondary precedence; profile matrices (modified by mode adjustments) take tertiary precedence; and unresolved or "off" profiles set all nodes to None to enable provider default behavior.

Parameters:

  • profile (str): Resolved profile name ("economy", "balanced", "quality", "max", or "off"). Must not be "auto".
  • mode (str): Active pipeline execution mode ("tutorial", "advanced", "sdk", or "api-reference").
  • global_level (str | None): Optional override setting all nodes to an identical level.
  • overrides (dict[str, str]): Node-specific override dictionary returned from parse_overrides().

Returns:

  • dict[str, str | None]: A complete plan dictionary mapping every key in NODE_KEYS to a level string or None.

Raises:

  • None directly.

Example:

# Implementation from utils/thinking.py
def build_thinking_plan(profile: str, mode: str, global_level: str | None, overrides: dict) -> dict:
    """Return {node_key: level | None} for every NODE key.

    Precedence: overrides > global_level > profile table (+ mode adjustments).
    `profile` must already be resolved (see resolve_profile_name).
    """
    if global_level:
        plan = dict.fromkeys(NODE_KEYS, global_level.lower())
    elif profile in _PROFILES:
        plan = dict(_PROFILES[profile])
        plan.update(_MODE_ADJUSTMENTS.get(profile, {}).get(mode, {}))
    else:  # "off": every node uses the model's default thinking behavior
        plan = dict.fromkeys(NODE_KEYS)
    plan.update(overrides)
    return plan

The plan synthesis proceeds through structured cascading branches. If global_level is set, all node keys are initialized to that value. If omitted and profile exists in _PROFILES, a shallow copy of the profile dictionary is loaded and updated with mode-specific adjustments from _MODE_ADJUSTMENTS. Otherwise, if the profile is "off", all keys are initialized with None. Finally, plan.update(overrides) is applied, ensuring node-specific CLI parameters overwrite baseline settings.

docs.title: resolve_thinking_level()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def resolve_thinking_level(shared: dict, node_key: str) -> str | None:

Description: Retrieves the resolved thinking level for a specific pipeline node at LLM call execution time. Inspects the thinking_plan dictionary stored within the application's shared runtime state; if absent or if the key is missing from the plan, it gracefully falls back to the legacy thinking_level attribute in the shared state.

Parameters:

  • shared (dict): The central shared context dictionary passed across pipeline nodes.
  • node_key (str): The unique identifier for the calling node (must align with NODE_KEYS).

Returns:

  • str | None: The designated thinking level string (e.g., "high"), or None if unconfigured or defaulting to model parameters.

Raises:

  • None directly.

Example:

# Implementation from utils/thinking.py
def resolve_thinking_level(shared: dict, node_key: str) -> str | None:
    """Thinking level for one LLM call site. Falls back to the global level when no plan exists."""
    plan = shared.get("thinking_plan")
    if plan and node_key in plan:
        return plan[node_key]
    return shared.get("thinking_level")

This helper guarantees backward compatibility during transitions between global thinking configurations and node-specific thinking flows. Downstream modules do not need to parse CLI flags or profile configurations directly; they provide their node key to retrieve their assigned budget.

docs.title: describe_plan()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public

Signature: def describe_plan(plan: dict, mode: str | None = None) -> str:

Description: Formats an active thinking plan into a compact, single-line comma-delimited string for startup logging and operational audit displays. Restricts rendering to the node keys relevant to the specified execution mode.

Parameters:

  • plan (dict[str, str | None]): The compiled thinking plan mapping node keys to levels.
  • mode (str | None): The active pipeline mode used to filter displayed nodes via MODE_NODES. If omitted or unrecognized, all NODE_KEYS are rendered.

Returns:

  • str: Comma-delimited key-value string (e.g., "filter_files=low, extract_facts=low, write_chapters=medium"). Unset or None levels are rendered as "default".

Raises:

  • None directly.

Example:

# Implementation from utils/thinking.py
def describe_plan(plan: dict, mode: str | None = None) -> str:
    """Compact one-line rendering for the startup config display (only nodes that run in `mode`)."""
    keys = MODE_NODES.get(mode, NODE_KEYS)
    return ", ".join(f"{key}={plan.get(key) or 'default'}" for key in keys)

The function interrogates MODE_NODES using the provided mode. By omitting irrelevant nodes (such as omitting heuristic analysis nodes in api-reference mode), it prevents log clutter and clarifies active inference parameters during system startup.

docs.title: _ANALYSIS_NODES
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _ANALYSIS_NODES = ("map_abstractions", "reduce_abstractions", "identify_abstractions", "analyze_relationships", "order_chapters")

Description: File-scoped constant defining the subset of pipeline nodes responsible for high-level heuristic abstraction and relationship analysis. Shared across narrative documentation modes (tutorial, advanced, sdk) to construct their corresponding entries in MODE_NODES.

# Definition in utils/thinking.py
_ANALYSIS_NODES = ("map_abstractions", "reduce_abstractions", "identify_abstractions", "analyze_relationships", "order_chapters")

These nodes represent the reasoning-intensive analytical phases that analyze raw source trees to extract domain concepts and plan architectural chapters.

docs.title: _PROFILES
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _PROFILES = { "economy": { ... }, "balanced": { ... }, "quality": { ... }, "max": { ... } }

Description: Internal configuration dictionary defining baseline thinking level assignments across all NODE_KEYS for each supported profile name.

# Base per-node levels. Reasoning-heavy synthesis (identify/reduce abstractions) gets the
# most effort; relationship analysis only feeds the summary, diagram and ordering, so it
# sits one level lower; long-form generation gets enough to plan accurately; mechanical
# transforms stay low.
_PROFILES = {
    "economy": {
        "filter_files": "low",
        "extract_facts": "low",
        "map_abstractions": "low",
        "reduce_abstractions": "medium",
        "identify_abstractions": "medium",
        "analyze_relationships": "low",
        "order_chapters": "low",
        "write_chapters": "low",
        "chapter_summary": "low",
        "group_modules": "low",
        "translate_strings": "low",
    },
    "balanced": {
        "filter_files": "low",
        "extract_facts": "low",
        "map_abstractions": "medium",
        "reduce_abstractions": "high",
        "identify_abstractions": "high",
        "analyze_relationships": "medium",
        "order_chapters": "medium",
        "write_chapters": "medium",
        "chapter_summary": "low",
        "group_modules": "medium",
        "translate_strings": "low",
    },
    "quality": {
        "filter_files": "medium",
        "extract_facts": "medium",
        "map_abstractions": "high",
        "reduce_abstractions": "high",
        "identify_abstractions": "high",
        "analyze_relationships": "high",
        "order_chapters": "high",
        "write_chapters": "high",
        "chapter_summary": "medium",
        "group_modules": "high",
        "translate_strings": "medium",
    },
    "max": {
        "filter_files": "medium",
        "extract_facts": "medium",
        "map_abstractions": "xhigh",
        "reduce_abstractions": "max",
        "identify_abstractions": "max",
        "analyze_relationships": "xhigh",
        "order_chapters": "high",
        "write_chapters": "xhigh",
        "chapter_summary": "medium",
        "group_modules": "high",
        "translate_strings": "medium",
    },
}

The matrix implements a deliberate economic strategy:

  1. Mechanical operations (filter_files, extract_facts, translate_strings) remain constrained to "low" or "medium" effort across all profiles.
  2. Context summarization (chapter_summary) remains at "low" or "medium" because summaries require short, concise prose rather than extensive planning.
  3. Core analytical synthesis (identify_abstractions, reduce_abstractions) receives the highest tier in every profile ("high" in balanced, "max" in max).
  4. Long-form drafting (write_chapters) scales conservatively ("medium" in balanced) because chapter writing executes repeatedly across $N$ abstractions, compounding token overhead.

docs.title: _MODE_ADJUSTMENTS
docs.text:
Visibility: Private

Signature: _MODE_ADJUSTMENTS = { "economy": {"advanced": {"write_chapters": "medium"}}, }

Description: Internal nested dictionary specifying mode-dependent overrides applied over baseline profiles. Compensates for documentation modes that demand higher reasoning capabilities even when executing under constrained profiles.

# Mode-specific adjustments on top of the base profile. advanced chapters carry design-
# rationale analysis and there are at most max_abstraction_num of them, so economy keeps
# them at medium instead of low.
_MODE_ADJUSTMENTS = {
    "economy": {"advanced": {"write_chapters": "medium"}},
}

Under the economy profile, baseline chapter writing is capped at "low". However, because advanced mode produces technical deep-dives detailing architectural design rationale and operates over a bounded number of abstractions, _MODE_ADJUSTMENTS raises write_chapters to "medium".

docs.title: Profile Matrix (_PROFILES)
docs.text:

docs.text:

The 2-tuple returned by parse_overrides() containing the structured mapping of valid overrides and an unparsed list of invalid elements.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
utils/thinking.py implements deterministic, non-throwing defensive validation patterns across all functions. Rather than raising runtime exceptions on malformed user inputs, functions sanitize values, collect diagnostic records, or fall back to safe default behaviors:

  • Override Syntax Validation: In parse_overrides(), candidate strings are partitioned around =. Any string lacking an = character, naming an unrecognized node, or designating an effort level outside THINKING_LEVELS is collected into the invalid return list. Execution proceeds without terminating the process, allowing callers to log warnings or exit cleanly.
  • Effort Level Clamping: In clamp_level(), if a requested level is absent from the target model's supported set, the function calculates absolute distance along THINKING_LEVELS. Equidistant ties resolve toward lower computational cost (min(ranked, key=lambda lvl: (abs(...), index))). If the requested level is completely unrecognized or supported has no overlap with THINKING_LEVELS, the function returns None rather than raising a ValueError or KeyError.
  • Missing Plan Fallbacks: In resolve_thinking_level(), if shared lacks a thinking_plan key or the target node_key is not present within the plan, the function falls back to retrieving shared.get("thinking_level"). If neither exists, it safely returns None, allowing inference adapters to fall back to native model defaults.
  • Profile Resolution Fallback: In resolve_profile_name(), empty or None inputs default to "auto". For providers not registered in PROFILED_PROVIDERS, "auto" gracefully degrades to "off", preventing uncalibrated providers from receiving unexpected reasoning configuration payloads.

docs.title: token_utils.py
docs.text: Source: utils/token_utils.py

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
utils/token_utils.py provides the token counting, prompt sizing, context window headroom budgeting, and dynamic token ratio calibration infrastructure for the codebase knowledge generation pipeline. Large language models (LLMs) across different vendors employ disparate tokenization schemes (such as Byte-Pair Encoding variants like cl100k_base, SentencePiece, or custom gemini/claude tokenizers). Because running vendor-specific tokenizers locally for every candidate prompt is computationally expensive or impossible without network round-trips, this module uses a fast local baseline (tiktoken's cl100k_base) paired with an adaptive calibration system that dynamically scales raw token counts to match the active model's billed token counts.

The architecture decouples raw token counting from model-specific token budgeting. Raw counts are computed using tiktoken with an in-memory, thread-safe LRU-style cache (OrderedDict) keyed by string length and content hash to eliminate redundant processing across execution phases. If tiktoken fails to load or environment constraints prevent downloading encoding files, the system falls back to a deterministic byte-ratio estimator (UTF-8 bytes / 3), which deliberately over-counts source code rather than under-counting multi-byte non-English scripts. The dynamic calibration engine observes provider-reported token usage across requests, applying an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) with size weighting to adjust the token multiplier. This learned ratio is persisted to disk in llm_token_calibration.json, ensuring subsequent workflow runs immediately benefit from calibrated headroom estimates.

Prompt budgeting logic computes the maximum safe prompt size that guarantees adequate headroom for model responses, chain-of-thought thinking tokens, and estimation uncertainty. Providers such as Anthropic and OpenRouter enforce shared context windows where prompt and completion tokens share the total limit, whereas Google Gemini maintains separated input and output quotas. The budgeting engine queries provider capabilities to reserve output space and scales down the uncertainty reserve from 5% to 2% once the active model's ratio is verified through real usage data.
